cells.tense: It's already finished, and you're standing here with your hands open.
cells.ask: Pick the one thing you've been holding past its finish and put it down where someone can pick it up — today, in the open — and let the space stay empty a week before you fill it.
cells.core:
You finished something and you can hold the fact of it. Most people can't find the end of a thing; you know what you carried, what it cost to carry, and you're here with it instead of pretending you're still in the middle. That's the whole thing working — a finished piece fully in hand, and the hand still open.

What comes next is release, and it's work, not surrender. The move is to notice what's done and give it over so the next thing has somewhere to land. If you can still feel a grip, that's habit, not failure, and it loosens when you say what's finished out loud and stop adding to it.
cells.sheetLine: What's finished is in your hands and the hands are open.
cells.verb: carrying what the beginning became to its end, then setting it down
cells.place: the table where what you've held is released

cells.tense: You'll manage the release before it happens, and you'll be braced for it the whole way.
cells.ask: Let one finished thing sit in the room past the point where you'd normally move it — don't hand it off, don't tidy it — and see what's there without your plan attached.
cells.core:
The clean version is simple: an ending arrives, you're in it, nothing is already decided, no next step named. The release happens because you were there for it, not because you'd prepared for it.

Right now you're ahead of the ending. A thing isn't finished and you've got the plan for it, the story of how it went, the next one lined up. Your attention lives up the road, so nothing ever quite lands. The release that would settle you is smaller than the plan: see what's finished as finished, with no next move attached. Let it be over before you decide what to do with it. Nothing has to happen right now.
cells.sheetLine: You're managing the ending before you've let the thing end.

cells.tense: You put it down a while back, but you're still hanging around the doorway.
cells.ask: Say out loud to one person what actually finished — plainly, no framing — then let them respond and don't correct it, add to it, or explain it afterward.
cells.core:
Letting something go and keeping on letting it go — knowing it's over and deepening that knowing as you move past it — is what this looks like when it's going well.

The putting-down already happened; you've just kept it in the past tense, going back over what it was and what you would have done. The thing isn't what holds you. It's the version of yourself that was still in it. What's starved here isn't effort — it's being received. Someone needs to actually hear what's done so it becomes finished in the world and not only in your head. Let it be witnessed instead of reviewed. An ending gets real when another person can see it.
cells.sheetLine: The door closed. Part of you is still in the doorway.

cells.tense: You're letting go of things all the time without ever calling it yours.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've released recently and say plainly that you chose to let it go — to one person, as your call, without crediting the situation or the timing.
cells.core:
You release things without noticing you're doing it. Plans, people, roles that stopped fitting — they've gone by the hand, and you talk about it like it happened to you. The situation changed. The timing was right. Someone else moved on.

What happened is real and it's yours. You keep describing it in the passive because claiming it means saying you ended things on purpose, and that sounds heavier than it is. It isn't heavier. It's just true. Own the release and you keep the same hands, and the next thing you pick up you pick up as someone who chose the last one's ending.

A reader could say the release they can't do isn't clinging at all, it's a plain unwillingness that has reasons. The ask survives being wrong: each one is a small physical act of letting a real thing leave the hand, useful even if the read is off. The sentence that serves me: any line that sounds like the card has already decided what they must give up — cut.
